name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q01 - Transport of substances in sponges and coelenterates

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups of organisms circulate water from their surroundings through their body cavities to facilitate the exchange of nutrients and gases by their cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different animal groups have evolved transport mechanisms suited to their body complexity. While higher organisms use specialised internal fluids such as blood and lymph, simple multicellular organisms rely on environmental water.

Step 2: Evaluation
Simple organisms like sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings through their body cavities so that cells can directly exchange nutrients, \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and waste substances.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sponges and coelenterates circulate surrounding water through their body cavities for substance exchange.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q02 - Composition of blood plasma

questiontext.text: Plasma constitutes nearly what percentage of human blood, and what percentage of plasma is composed of water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood is a special connective tissue consisting of a fluid matrix called plasma and formed elements.

Step 2: Quantitative Facts
Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid that constitutes nearly \(55\%\) of the blood. Within plasma, \(90\text{--}92\%\) is water and \(6\text{--}8\%\) is contributed by proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plasma constitutes nearly \(55\%\) of blood, and \(90\text{--}92\%\) of plasma is water.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q03 - Functions of major plasma proteins

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs the major plasma proteins with their primary physiological functions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins contribute \(6\text{--}8\%\) of plasma, with fibrinogen, globulins, and albumins being the three major types.

Step 2: Function Mapping
Fibrinogens are needed for clotting or coagulation of blood. Globulins are primarily involved in defense mechanisms of the body. Albumins help maintain osmotic balance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fibrinogen functions in blood coagulation, globulins in defense mechanisms, and albumins in osmotic balance.

answer.text: Fibrinogen: osmotic balance; Globulins: clotting; Albumins: defense
Fibrinogen: defense; Globulins: osmotic balance; Albumins: clotting
Fibrinogen: clotting; Globulins: defense; Albumins: osmotic balance
Fibrinogen: gas transport; Globulins: clotting; Albumins: defense

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q04 - Definition of serum

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately defines blood serum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasma contains factors for coagulation or clotting of blood in an inactive form.

Step 2: Evaluation
When clotting factors are removed from plasma, the remaining fluid is called serum. It still retains water, minerals, albumins, globulins, and nutrients in transit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q05 - Minerals and transit substances in plasma

questiontext.text: Besides water and proteins, which of the following sets of substances are normally present in human blood plasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasma serves as the fluid medium transporting electrolytes and nutrients throughout the body.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plasma contains small amounts of minerals such as \(\mathrm{Na^+}\), \(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\), \(\mathrm{Mg^{++}}\), \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\), and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), as well as glucose, amino acids, and lipids because these nutrients are always in transit in the body. Haemoglobin is confined inside RBCs, not free in plasma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plasma normally contains \(\mathrm{Na^+}\), \(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\), \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\), glucose, amino acids, and lipids.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q06 - Physiological consequence of albumin deficiency

questiontext.text: A patient exhibits a marked reduction in plasma albumin concentration while fibrinogen and globulin levels remain normal. Which physiological process in the blood is most directly impaired?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The three major plasma proteins have distinct, non-overlapping primary functions: fibrinogen in coagulation, globulins in defense, and albumins in osmotic balance.

Step 2: Evaluation
A selective reduction in plasma albumin directly impairs the osmotic balance of blood, whereas clotting (fibrinogen and clotting factors) and antibody-mediated defense (globulins) depend on the other plasma proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Maintenance of osmotic balance is most directly impaired by a reduction in plasma albumin.

answer.text: Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin during coagulation
Maintenance of osmotic balance of the blood

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q07 - Proportion and components of formed elements

questiontext.text: Erythrocytes, leucocytes, and platelets are collectively called formed elements, and they constitute nearly what percentage of human blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human blood consists of two major fractions: fluid matrix (plasma) and cellular components (formed elements).

Step 2: Evaluation
While plasma constitutes nearly \(55\%\) of blood, the formed elements (erythrocytes, leucocytes, and platelets) constitute nearly \(45\%\) of blood.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Formed elements constitute nearly \(45\%\) of human blood.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q08 - Normal RBC count and site of formation

questiontext.text: In a healthy adult man, the average number of erythrocytes per \(\text{mm}^3\) of blood and their primary site of formation are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Erythrocytes (RBCs) are the most abundant cells in human blood.

Step 2: Quantitative and Anatomical Facts
A healthy adult man has on average \(5\text{ to }5.5\ \text{millions}\) of RBCs \(\text{mm}^{-3}\) of blood, and in adults they are formed in the red bone marrow.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The average RBC count is \(5\text{--}5.5\ \text{millions mm}^{-3}\) and their site of formation in adults is the red bone marrow.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q09 - Haemoglobin concentration and RBC lifespan

questiontext.text: What is the normal haemoglobin content in every \(100\ \text{mL}\) of blood of a healthy individual, and what is the average life span of an erythrocyte before destruction in the spleen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
RBCs contain the red-coloured, iron-containing complex protein haemoglobin, which plays a major role in respiratory gas transport.

Step 2: Evaluation
A healthy individual has \(12\text{--}16\ \text{g}\) of haemoglobin in every \(100\ \text{mL}\) of blood. RBCs have an average life span of \(120\ \text{days}\), after which they are destroyed in the spleen (the graveyard of RBCs).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Normal haemoglobin content is \(12\text{--}16\ \text{g per }100\ \text{mL}\) of blood, and the average RBC life span is \(120\ \text{days}\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q10 - Classification of leucocytes into granulocytes and agranulocytes

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups correctly lists only the granulocytes among human leucocytes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leucocytes (WBCs) are nucleated, colourless cells averaging \(6000\text{--}8000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\) of blood, divided into two main categories: granulocytes and agranulocytes.

Step 2: Classification
Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are the three types of granulocytes, whereas lymphocytes and monocytes are the two types of agranulocytes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are granulocytes.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q11 - Most and least abundant leucocytes

questiontext.text: Which pair represents the most abundant and the least abundant types of white blood cells, respectively, in normal human blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The five types of WBCs occur in characteristic relative proportions of the total leucocyte count.

Step 2: Quantitative Comparison
Neutrophils constitute \(60\text{--}65\%\) of total WBCs (most abundant), followed by lymphocytes (\(20\text{--}25\%\)), monocytes (\(6\text{--}8\%\)), eosinophils (\(2\text{--}3\%\)), and basophils (\(0.5\text{--}1\%\), least abundant).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neutrophils are the most abundant and basophils are the least abundant WBCs.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q12 - Phagocytic white blood cells

questiontext.text: Which two types of leucocytes act as phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms entering the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phagocytosis is a key innate defense mechanism carried out by specialised leucocytes that engulf and destroy invading microbes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neutrophils (\(60\text{--}65\%\)) and monocytes (\(6\text{--}8\%\)) are phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms entering the body. Basophils mediate inflammatory reactions, eosinophils resist infections and mediate allergic reactions, and lymphocytes mediate specific B and T immune responses.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neutrophils and monocytes are the phagocytic leucocytes.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q13 - Secretions and role of basophils

questiontext.text: Which type of granulocyte secretes histamine, serotonin, and heparin, and is involved in inflammatory reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each granulocyte type releases specific mediators during immune and inflammatory responses.

Step 2: Evaluation
Basophils (\(0.5\text{--}1\%\) of total WBCs) secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin, etc., and participate in inflammatory reactions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Basophils secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin and are involved in inflammatory reactions.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q14 - Role of eosinophils and lymphocytes

questiontext.text: During an allergic reaction, which leucocyte type is specifically associated with resisting infections and mediating the allergic response?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different WBCs have specialised functions in immunity, phagocytosis, inflammation, and allergy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Eosinophils (\(2\text{--}3\%\) of total WBCs) resist infections and are also associated with allergic reactions. B and T lymphocytes (\(20\text{--}25\%\)) mediate adaptive immune responses, while neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Eosinophils are associated with resisting infections and allergic reactions.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q15 - Origin and normal count of platelets

questiontext.text: Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments produced from which specialised cells in the bone marrow, and what is their normal count per \(\text{mm}^3\) of blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Platelets release substances involved in blood coagulation; a reduction in their number can cause clotting disorders and excessive blood loss.

Step 2: Evaluation
Platelets are cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes (special cells in the bone marrow), and human blood normally contains \(1,50,000\text{--}3,50,000\) platelets \(\text{mm}^{-3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Platelets originate from megakaryocytes and normally number \(1,50,000\text{--}3,50,000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q16 - Calculation of neutrophil and basophil counts

questiontext.text: A healthy individual has a total leucocyte count of \(7000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\) of blood. Based on normal percentage ranges, what is the expected range of neutrophils and basophils, respectively, per \(\text{mm}^3\) of blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total WBC count \(= 7000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\). Normal percentage of neutrophils \(= 60\text{--}65\%\); normal percentage of basophils \(= 0.5\text{--}1\%\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Cell count} = \frac{\text{Percentage}}{100} \times \text{Total WBC count}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
For neutrophils: Lower bound \(= \frac{60}{100} \times 7000 = 4200\ \text{mm}^{-3}\). Upper bound \(= \frac{65}{100} \times 7000 = 4550\ \text{mm}^{-3}\). For basophils: Lower bound \(= \frac{0.5}{100} \times 7000 = 35\ \text{mm}^{-3}\). Upper bound \(= \frac{1}{100} \times 7000 = 70\ \text{mm}^{-3}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both ranges sum consistently within total WBC proportions. The expected counts are \(4200\text{--}4550\ \text{mm}^{-3}\) for neutrophils and \(35\text{--}70\ \text{mm}^{-3}\) for basophils.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q17 - Basis of ABO blood grouping

questiontext.text: The ABO blood grouping system in humans is based on the presence or absence of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood groups classify individuals based on immunologically distinct molecules on erythrocytes and corresponding antibodies in plasma.

Step 2: Evaluation
ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens—A and B—on the RBCs, accompanied by natural antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in the plasma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens (A and B) on RBCs.

answer.text: Two surface antigens, A and B, on the RBCs
Two surface antigens, A and B, on the platelets

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q18 - Reason why group O is the universal donor

questiontext.text: Why are individuals with blood group O referred to as universal donors in the ABO system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During blood transfusion, clumping (destruction of donor RBCs) occurs if the recipient's plasma antibodies react with antigens on the donor's RBCs.

Step 2: Evaluation
RBCs of blood group O have neither A nor B surface antigens (nil antigens), so they will not be clumped by anti-A or anti-B antibodies in any recipient's plasma. Hence, group O blood can be donated to persons of any ABO blood group.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Group O individuals are universal donors because their RBCs lack both A and B surface antigens.

answer.text: Their plasma lacks both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Their RBCs lack both A and B surface antigens
Their RBCs carry both A and B surface antigens

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q19 - Donor compatibility for blood group B recipient

questiontext.text: A patient with blood group B requires a blood transfusion. Assuming Rh compatibility, which ABO blood groups can safely donate blood to this patient?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A recipient's plasma antibodies must not react with the donor's RBC surface antigens to avoid clumping.

Step 2: Evaluation
An individual with blood group B has antigen B on RBCs and anti-A antibodies in plasma. Therefore, donor RBCs must not carry antigen A. Both group B (antigen B) and group O (no antigens) lack antigen A, whereas groups A and AB carry antigen A and would cause clumping.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A recipient with blood group B can safely receive blood from donors of groups B and O.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q20 - Rh antigen prevalence and transfusion response

questiontext.text: Nearly what percentage of humans are Rh positive (\(\text{Rh+ve}\)), and what happens if an Rh negative (\(\text{Rh-ve}\)) person is exposed to \(\text{Rh+ve}\) blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Rh antigen, similar to one present in Rhesus monkeys, is another surface antigen on human RBCs that must be matched prior to blood transfusions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nearly \(80\%\) of humans possess the Rh antigen on their RBCs (\(\text{Rh+ve}\)). An \(\text{Rh-ve}\) person lacks this antigen and, if exposed to \(\text{Rh+ve}\) blood, will form specific antibodies against the Rh antigens.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nearly \(80\%\) of humans are \(\text{Rh+ve}\), and an \(\text{Rh-ve}\) person exposed to \(\text{Rh+ve}\) blood forms specific antibodies against Rh antigens.

answer.text: \(20\%\); the person destroys their own platelets
\(80\%\); the person forms specific antibodies against Rh antigens

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q21 - Mechanism of erythroblastosis foetalis

questiontext.text: Why does erythroblastosis foetalis typically affect subsequent pregnancies rather than the first pregnancy in an \(\text{Rh-ve}\) mother carrying an \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Erythroblastosis foetalis is caused by Rh incompatibility between an \(\text{Rh-ve}\) mother and an \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetus.

Step 2: Evaluation
During the first pregnancy, the foetal and maternal bloods are well separated by the placenta, so foetal Rh antigens are not exposed to maternal blood. During delivery of the first child, maternal blood may be exposed to small amounts of \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetal blood, causing the mother to prepare anti-Rh antibodies. In subsequent pregnancies, these maternal Rh antibodies can leak into the \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetal blood and destroy foetal RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The placenta separates maternal and foetal blood during the first pregnancy, and maternal sensitisation to Rh antigens typically occurs during the delivery of the first child.

answer.text: The placenta separates maternal and foetal blood during the first pregnancy, and maternal sensitisation occurs during delivery of the first child
The first foetus does not yet express Rh antigens on its RBCs until birth
Maternal anti-Rh antibodies are only produced during the second trimester of the second pregnancy
The \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetus produces antibodies against the mother's \(\text{Rh-ve}\) RBCs

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q22 - Prevention of erythroblastosis foetalis

questiontext.text: How can erythroblastosis foetalis be prevented in an \(\text{Rh-ve}\) mother who has just delivered her first \(\text{Rh+ve}\) child?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Preventing erythroblastosis foetalis requires stopping the \(\text{Rh-ve}\) mother from producing her own anti-Rh antibodies after exposure to \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetal blood at delivery.

Step 2: Evaluation
Administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child prevents her from preparing antibodies against the Rh antigen, thereby protecting subsequent \(\text{Rh+ve}\) foetuses.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery prevents erythroblastosis foetalis.

answer.text: By transfusing \(\text{Rh+ve}\) blood into the mother before the second pregnancy
By administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child
By administering Rh antigens to the newborn immediately after birth
By removing platelets from the maternal circulation

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q23 - Formation of fibrin clot

questiontext.text: During blood coagulation, the dark reddish-brown clot formed at an injury site consists mainly of a network of threads called fibrins, which are produced by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coagulation prevents excessive blood loss by forming a meshwork of insoluble fibrin threads that trap dead and damaged formed elements.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fibrins are formed by the conversion of inactive fibrinogens present in the plasma by the active enzyme thrombin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fibrins are produced by the conversion of inactive plasma fibrinogens by thrombin.

answer.text: Conversion of albumin into globulins by heparin
Conversion of prothrombin into fibrinogen by platelets
Conversion of inactive fibrinogens in plasma by the enzyme thrombin
Direct polymerisation of calcium ions in serum

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q24 - Role of thrombokinase and calcium ions in clotting

questiontext.text: Which enzyme complex formed by a cascade of linked enzymatic reactions converts inactive prothrombin into thrombin, and which mineral ion plays a very important role in blood clotting?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood coagulation is initiated by factors released from stimulated platelets and injured tissues, triggering a cascade process involving inactive plasma factors.

Step 2: Evaluation
The cascade of linked enzymatic reactions forms the enzyme complex thrombokinase, which converts inactive prothrombin in the plasma into thrombin. Calcium ions (\(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\)) play a very important role in clotting.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thrombokinase converts prothrombin into thrombin, and calcium ions play an essential role in clotting.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q25 - Interstitial fluid formation and mineral distribution

questiontext.text: How does the mineral distribution of interstitial (tissue) fluid compare with that of blood plasma, and what stays behind in the blood vessels during its formation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As blood passes through tissue capillaries, water and small water-soluble substances filter out into intercellular spaces to form interstitial fluid, through which exchange of nutrients and gases occurs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Interstitial fluid has the same mineral distribution as that in plasma, while larger proteins and most of the formed elements are left behind in the blood vessels.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Interstitial fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in the blood vessels.

answer.text: Same mineral distribution as plasma; larger proteins and most formed elements remain in blood vessels
No minerals present; erythrocytes and platelets move out into tissue spaces
Higher protein concentration than plasma; water remains inside capillaries
Same mineral distribution as plasma; only platelets and fibrinogen move out

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q26 - Lymphatic system drainage and immune role

questiontext.text: Where does the lymphatic system drain collected interstitial fluid, and which specialised cells in lymph are responsible for immune responses of the body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The lymphatic system is an elaborate network of vessels that collects tissue fluid (called lymph once inside the lymphatic vessels) and returns it to the blood vascular system.

Step 2: Evaluation
The lymphatic system drains collected fluid back into the major veins. Lymph is a colourless fluid containing specialised lymphocytes responsible for the immune responses of the body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The lymphatic system drains lymph back to the major veins, and specialised lymphocytes in lymph mediate immune responses.

answer.text: Back to the major veins; specialised lymphocytes

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q27 - Absorption of fats through lacteals

questiontext.text: In the human digestive tract, fats are absorbed through lymph in which specialised structures located in the intestinal villi?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Besides immunity and fluid return, lymph is an important carrier for nutrients and hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals of the intestinal villi.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q28 - Open versus closed circulatory systems

questiontext.text: Which pair of animal phyla exhibits an open circulatory system in which blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces called sinuses?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Circulatory patterns are broadly classified as open or closed.

Step 2: Evaluation
An open circulatory system is present in arthropods and molluscs, where blood enters open spaces or body cavities called sinuses. Annelids and chordates have a closed circulatory system, which allows more precise regulation of fluid flow.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Arthropods and molluscs exhibit an open circulatory system.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q29 - Single circulation in fishes

questiontext.text: In fishes, which type of blood does the 2-chambered heart pump out, and where is it oxygenated before reaching the body parts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fishes possess a 2-chambered heart with one atrium and one ventricle, exhibiting single circulation.

Step 2: Evaluation
In fishes, the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills and then supplied directly to the body parts, from where deoxygenated blood returns to the heart.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The fish heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q30 - Incomplete double circulation and crocodile exception

questiontext.text: Which of the following vertebrates is an exception among reptiles because it possesses a 4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles rather than a 3-chambered heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amphibians and most reptiles have a 3-chambered heart (two atria and a single ventricle) exhibiting incomplete double circulation, in which oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the single ventricle.

Step 2: Evaluation
Crocodiles, along with birds and mammals, possess a 4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles, making crocodiles the exception among reptiles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Crocodiles possess a 4-chambered heart.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q31 - Origin and protective covering of human heart

questiontext.text: The human heart is derived from which embryonic germ layer, and what is the double-walled membranous bag that protects it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human heart is situated in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is roughly the size of a clenched fist.

Step 2: Evaluation
The heart is a mesodermally derived organ protected by a double-walled membranous bag called the pericardium, which encloses the pericardial fluid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The human heart is mesodermally derived and protected by the pericardium.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q32 - Bicuspid (mitral) valve location

questiontext.text: The opening between the left atrium and the left ventricle in the human heart is guarded by which valve?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heart valves ensure unidirectional blood flow from atria to ventricles and from ventricles to major arteries.

Step 2: Evaluation
The tricuspid valve (three muscular flaps or cusps) guards the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle, whereas the bicuspid or mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle. Semilunar valves guard the openings of the ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q33 - Comparison of cardiac septa and chamber wall thickness

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the septa and chamber walls of the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four chambers of the human heart are separated by septa of distinct tissue compositions and thicknesses suited to their pumping pressures.

Step 2: Evaluation
The inter-atrial septum is a thin muscular wall separating the right and left atria, the inter-ventricular septum is thick-walled separating the right and left ventricles, and the atrio-ventricular septum is made of thick fibrous tissue. Furthermore, the walls of the ventricles are much thicker than those of the atria.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The inter-atrial septum is thin and muscular, the atrio-ventricular septum is thick fibrous tissue, and ventricular walls are much thicker than atrial walls.

answer.text: The inter-atrial septum is thin and muscular, the atrio-ventricular septum is thick fibrous tissue, and ventricular walls are much thicker than atrial walls
The inter-ventricular septum is thin and fibrous, whereas atrial walls are thicker than ventricular walls
The inter-atrial septum is thick fibrous tissue with no openings, while the atrio-ventricular septum is thin and muscular
All cardiac septa are composed exclusively of thin elastic fibres without any openings

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q34 - Anatomical locations of SAN and AVN

questiontext.text: Where are the sino-atrial node (SAN) and the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) located in the human heart?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Specialised cardiac musculature called nodal tissue is distributed in specific regions of the right atrium and ventricles.

Step 2: Evaluation
The sino-atrial node (SAN) is a patch of nodal tissue in the right upper corner of the right atrium, whereas the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) is a mass of nodal tissue in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
SAN is in the right upper corner of the right atrium, and AVN is in the lower left corner of the right atrium.

answer.text: SAN in the left atrium; AVN in the left ventricle
SAN in the right upper corner of the right atrium; AVN in the lower left corner of the right atrium
SAN in the inter-ventricular septum; AVN in the right upper corner of the right atrium
SAN in the lower left corner of the left atrium; AVN in the apex of the heart

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q35 - Autoexcitability and ventricular impulse conduction

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately explains how the action potential generated by the SAN reaches the entire ventricular musculature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nodal musculature is autoexcitable, generating action potentials without external stimuli, and conducts impulses from the atria to the ventricles.

Step 2: Evaluation
After the SAN stimulates atrial systole, the action potential is conducted to the ventricular side by the AVN and AV bundle (bundle of His), which passes through the atrio-ventricular septa to the top of the inter-ventricular septum, divides into right and left bundles, and gives rise to minute Purkinje fibres throughout the ventricular musculature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The impulse travels from the AVN through the AV bundle (bundle of His) and its right and left branches to the Purkinje fibres throughout the ventricular musculature.

answer.text: It passes directly across the fibrous atrio-ventricular septum without involving the AVN
It is transmitted via sympathetic nerves directly from the SAN to the Purkinje fibres
It is conducted by the AVN and AV bundle (bundle of His) to right and left branches and Purkinje fibres
It travels from the Purkinje fibres backwards to the AVN and then to the ventricular walls

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q36 - Contribution of atrial systole to ventricular filling

questiontext.text: During the cardiac cycle, simultaneous contraction of both atria (atrial systole) increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by approximately what percentage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During joint diastole, blood already flows passively from the pulmonary veins and vena cava into the ventricles through open tricuspid and bicuspid valves.

Step 2: Evaluation
When the SAN generates an action potential, both atria undergo simultaneous contraction (atrial systole), which increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about \(30\%\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Atrial systole increases ventricular blood flow by about \(30\%\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q37 - Duration of a cardiac cycle calculation

questiontext.text: If an individual's heart beats \(75\text{ times per minute}\), what is the duration of a single cardiac cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Heart rate \(= 75\ \text{beats min}^{-1}\), meaning \(75\) cardiac cycles are performed in \(60\ \text{s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Duration of one cardiac cycle} = \frac{60\ \text{s}}{\text{Heart rate (cycles per min)}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\(\text{Duration} = \frac{60}{75}\ \text{s} = \frac{4}{5}\ \text{s} = 0.8\ \text{s}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
At \(72\text{--}75\ \text{beats min}^{-1}\), each cardiac cycle lasts approximately \(0.8\ \text{s}\). Thus, the duration is \(0.8\ \text{s}\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q38 - Calculation of cardiac output in an athlete

questiontext.text: During exercise, an athlete's stroke volume is \(90\ \text{mL}\) and heart rate is \(80\ \text{beats min}^{-1}\). What is the athlete's cardiac output?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Stroke volume \(= 90\ \text{mL}\); Heart rate \(= 80\ \text{beats min}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Cardiac output} = \text{Stroke volume} \times \text{Heart rate}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\(\text{Cardiac output} = 90\ \text{mL} \times 80\ \text{min}^{-1} = 7200\ \text{mL min}^{-1}\). Converting to litres: \(\frac{7200}{1000} = 7.2\ \text{L min}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
This exceeds the resting average of \(\approx 5\ \text{L min}^{-1}\), which is expected for an athlete. The cardiac output is \(7.2\ \text{L min}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q39 - Origin of the two prominent heart sounds

questiontext.text: During each cardiac cycle, the first heart sound (lub) and the second heart sound (dub) heard through a stethoscope are associated respectively with the closure of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Two prominent heart sounds of clinical diagnostic significance are produced by the closure of cardiac valves during each cardiac cycle.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first heart sound (lub) is associated with the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves (at the start of ventricular systole), whereas the second heart sound (dub) is associated with the closure of the semilunar valves (at the start of ventricular diastole).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lub is caused by closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, and dub by closure of the semilunar valves.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q40 - Electrical lead placement for a standard ECG

questiontext.text: To obtain a standard electrocardiogram (ECG), three electrical leads are connected to which sites on a patient's body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electrocardiograph records the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface using electrical leads.

Step 2: Evaluation
For a standard ECG, a patient is connected to the machine with three electrical leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle. Multiple chest leads are added only for a detailed evaluation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A standard ECG uses three leads connected to each wrist and the left ankle.

answer.text: One to each ankle and one to the left wrist
Three leads attached directly to the chest region
One to each wrist and one to the right ankle
One to each wrist and one to the left ankle

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q41 - Significance of P-wave, QRS complex, and T-wave

questiontext.text: In a standard ECG, which statement accurately relates the electrical waves to mechanical events of the cardiac cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each peak in a standard ECG (P, Q, R, S, T) corresponds to a specific electrical activity of the heart that precedes or marks a mechanical contraction or relaxation phase.

Step 2: Evaluation
The P-wave represents atrial depolarisation leading to atrial contraction. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation initiating ventricular contraction (shortly after Q, marking the beginning of systole), and counting QRS complexes gives the heart rate. The T-wave represents ventricular repolarisation, and the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ventricular contraction begins shortly after Q, and the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.

answer.text: Ventricular contraction starts shortly after Q, and the end of the T-wave marks the end of systole
The P-wave represents ventricular repolarisation, and the T-wave represents atrial contraction
Counting the number of T-waves per minute cannot reflect heart rate, whereas P-wave marks end of systole
The QRS complex represents atrial depolarisation, marking the end of joint diastole

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q42 - Pathway of pulmonary circulation

questiontext.text: In human double circulation, which pathway accurately represents the pulmonary circulation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Humans have complete double circulation consisting of two separate pathways: pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pulmonary circulation begins when deoxygenated blood is pumped by the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, carried to the lungs for oxygenation, and returned as oxygenated blood via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs and back via pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

answer.text: Left ventricle \(\rightarrow\) aorta \(\rightarrow\) lungs \(\rightarrow\) vena cava \(\rightarrow\) right atrium
Right ventricle \(\rightarrow\) pulmonary artery \(\rightarrow\) lungs \(\rightarrow\) pulmonary veins \(\rightarrow\) left atrium
Right atrium \(\rightarrow\) pulmonary veins \(\rightarrow\) lungs \(\rightarrow\) pulmonary artery \(\rightarrow\) left ventricle
Left ventricle \(\rightarrow\) pulmonary artery \(\rightarrow\) body tissues \(\rightarrow\) vena cava \(\rightarrow\) right atrium

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q43 - Pathway of systemic circulation

questiontext.text: In systemic circulation, oxygenated blood is pumped out by which chamber of the heart, and deoxygenated blood from body tissues is emptied into which chamber?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Systemic circulation supplies nutrients, \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and other essential substances to body tissues and removes \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and wastes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Oxygenated blood is pumped by the left ventricle into the aorta and distributed via arteries, arterioles, and capillaries to tissues. Deoxygenated blood is collected by venules, veins, and vena cava and emptied into the right atrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Systemic circulation begins at the left ventricle and returns blood to the right atrium.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q44 - Hepatic portal system and coronary circulation

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes the hepatic portal system from the coronary system in humans?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Humans possess specialised vascular connections in addition to the main pulmonary and systemic circuits.

Step 2: Evaluation
The hepatic portal system is a unique vascular connection between the digestive tract and the liver, where the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system of blood vessels exists exclusively for the circulation of blood to and from the cardiac musculature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver, whereas the coronary system circulates blood exclusively to and from the cardiac musculature.

answer.text: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the liver to the lungs, whereas the coronary system supplies the kidneys
The hepatic portal system drains lymph into the vena cava, whereas the coronary system drains intestinal villi
The hepatic portal vein carries oxygenated blood from the aorta to the intestine, whereas the coronary system supplies skeletal muscles
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before systemic circulation, whereas the coronary system circulates blood exclusively to and from the cardiac musculature

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q45 - Neural and hormonal regulation of cardiac activity

questiontext.text: Which combination accurately describes the moderation of human cardiac function by the neural centre in the medulla oblongata and adrenal medullary hormones?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although the human heart is myogenic (auto-regulated by nodal tissue), a special neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates cardiac activity via the autonomic nervous system (ANS), alongside hormonal influences.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sympathetic neural signals increase heart rate, strength of ventricular contraction, and cardiac output. Parasympathetic neural signals decrease heart rate, speed of conduction of action potential, and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sympathetic nerves and adrenal medullary hormones increase cardiac output, whereas parasympathetic nerves decrease heart rate, conduction speed, and cardiac output.

answer.text: Sympathetic nerves and adrenal medullary hormones increase cardiac output, whereas parasympathetic nerves decrease heart rate and conduction speed
Parasympathetic nerves and adrenal medullary hormones increase cardiac output, whereas sympathetic nerves decrease heart rate
Both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves decrease the strength of ventricular contraction
Adrenal medullary hormones decrease cardiac output, while the medulla oblongata has no role in cardiac regulation

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q46 - Normal blood pressure and hypertension criteria

questiontext.text: In standard blood pressure measurement (\(120/80\ \text{mm Hg}\)), what do the two values represent, and what repeated reading indicates hypertension?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hypertension refers to blood pressure higher than normal, which can lead to heart disease and damage vital organs such as the brain and kidneys.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(120/80\ \text{mm Hg}\), \(120\ \text{mm Hg}\) is the systolic (pumping) pressure and \(80\ \text{mm Hg}\) is the diastolic (resting) pressure. Repeated checks of \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher indicate hypertension.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(120\ \text{mm Hg}\) is systolic pressure, \(80\ \text{mm Hg}\) is diastolic pressure, and repeated readings of \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher indicate hypertension.

answer.text: \(120\): diastolic pressure; \(80\): systolic pressure; hypertension: \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher
\(120\): systolic pressure; \(80\): diastolic pressure; hypertension: \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher
\(120\): systolic pressure; \(80\): diastolic pressure; hypertension: \(120/80\ \text{mm Hg}\)
\(120\): venous pressure; \(80\): arterial pressure; hypertension: \(100/70\ \text{mm Hg}\)

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q47 - Coronary Artery Disease and Angina pectoris

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) and angina pectoris?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inadequate blood and oxygen supply to the cardiac musculature underlies both atherosclerosis (CAD) and angina pectoris.

Step 2: Evaluation
Coronary Artery Disease (atherosclerosis) narrows the lumen of arteries supplying the heart muscle due to deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissues. Angina pectoris is a symptom of acute chest pain that appears when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle due to conditions affecting blood flow.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
CAD narrows coronary arteries via calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissue deposits, while angina pectoris is acute chest pain caused by insufficient oxygen reaching the heart muscle.

answer.text: CAD is caused by congestion of the lungs, whereas angina is caused by a complete halt in heartbeat
CAD widens the arterial lumen due to fibrin loss, whereas angina occurs only in infants
CAD narrows coronary arteries via deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissues, while angina is acute chest pain when insufficient oxygen reaches the heart muscle
CAD affects only the pulmonary veins, while angina results from excess oxygen in the myocardium

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MCQ_Q48 - Distinction between heart failure, cardiac arrest, and heart attack

questiontext.text: How does heart failure (congestive heart failure) differ from cardiac arrest and a heart attack?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although often confused, heart failure, cardiac arrest, and heart attack represent distinct clinical states of the heart.

Step 2: Evaluation
Heart failure is the state when the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the needs of the body, often termed congestive heart failure because lung congestion is a main symptom. By contrast, cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating, and a heart attack is when the heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heart failure is ineffective pumping to meet body needs (with lung congestion), whereas cardiac arrest is cessation of heartbeat and a heart attack is sudden myocardial damage from inadequate blood supply.

answer.text: Heart failure is when the heart stops beating completely, whereas cardiac arrest is lung congestion
Heart failure and heart attack are identical terms for sudden damage to the heart muscle
Heart failure is elevated blood pressure above \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\), whereas cardiac arrest is chest pain

Heart failure is ineffective pumping to meet body needs (often with lung congestion), whereas cardiac arrest is when the heart stops beating and heart attack is sudden muscle damage from inadequate blood supply
